These results store details related to the extracted entities, including the sentenceindex and the position of the mentions in the text, by specifying the start and endcharacters. In addition to information entities such as types and aliases, thesedetails will be used to perform advanced queries, as discussed in section 7.7. Nowwe can load the results into Neo4j.

Listing 7.13 Loading NED data
[...] 
class NLPImporter(BaseImporter): 
[...] 
 
  def load_nlp_res(self): 
    print("Loading data into Neo4j...") 
    with open(self.file,'rb') as file: 
    processed_pages = pickle.load(file) 
 
    query = """ 
            UNWIND $rows as item 
 
            MATCH (page:Page)   #1 
            WHERE page.id = item.id AND NOT page:NEDProcessed 
            SET page:NEDProcessed 
            WITH page, item 
 
            UNWIND item.ents as entity 
            MERGE ( 
              mention:EntityMention { 
                name_normalized: toLower( 
                  apoc.text.join( 
                    apoc.text.split(trim(entity.value), "\\s+"), " " 
                  ) 
                ) 
              } 
            )   #2 
            ON CREATE SET  
              mention.name = apoc.text.join( 
                apoc.text.split(trim(entity.value), "\\s+"), " " 
             ) 
            MERGE  
  (page)-[s:MENTIONS_MENTION {from_model: "ned"}]->(mention)   #3 
 
            ON CREATE SET s.start_chars= [entity.beginCharacter],  
                        s.end_chars= [entity.endCharacter],  
                        s.sentence_index = [entity.sentenceIndex], 
                        s.type = toLower(entity.label) 
            ON MATCH SET s.start_chars = s.start_chars + entity.beginChar
acter, 
                        s.end_chars = s.end_chars + entity.endCharacter,  
                        s.sentence_index = s.sentence_index + 
                        ↪ entity.sentenceIndex 
            WITH page, mention, entity      
 

            FOREACH(medical in entity | 
            MERGE (dis:MedicalEntity {id: medical.selected_ned_id})  #4 
            ON CREATE SET dis.name= 
            ↪ apoc.text.join(apoc.text.split(trim(medical.selected_ned_nam
e), 
            ↪ "\\s+"), " "), 
                        dis.type_id = medical.selected_ned_types_id,  
                        dis.types = medical.selected_ned_types, 
                        dis.type = medical.selected_ned_types[0], 
                        dis.original_mention = medical.value,  
                        dis.definition = medical.selected_ned_definition,  
                        dis.aliases = medical.selected_ned_aliases, 
                        dis.start_chars= [entity.beginCharacter],  
                        dis.end_chars= [entity.endCharacter],  
                        dis.sentence_index = [entity.sentenceIndex]  #5 
            ON MATCH SET dis.start_chars = dis.start_chars + 
            ↪ entity.beginCharacter,  
                        dis.end_chars = dis.end_chars + entity.endCharact
er 
 
            MERGE (mention)-[r:DISAMBIGUATED_TO]->(dis)  #6 
            SET r.confidence = medical.selected_ned.confidence 
 
            MERGE (page)-[t:MENTIONS_ENTITY]->(dis)  #7 
            ON CREATE SET t.sentence_index = [medical.sentenceIndex] 
            ON MATCH SET t.sentence_index = t.sentence_index + 
            ↪ medical.sentenceIndex)   
 
            """ 
 
        self.load_in_batch(query, processed_pages, len(processed_pages), 
   ↪ chunk_size=1)
#1 Matches node pages that are not yet processed #2 Creates entity mention nodes and connects them to pages #3 Adds properties, including start and end chars, to relationships connecting pages and mentions #4 Merges medical entity nodes extracted using the scispaCy tool #5 Adds properties, including aliases and semantic types, to the medical entity nodes #6 Connects medical entity nodes to entity mentions #7 Connects medical entity nodes to pages 
This query stores the results of scispaCy processing in Neo4j. First it creates the
EntityMention nodes, which are connected to the Page nodes. Then it creates the
MedicalEntity nodes, enriches them with UMLS data, and connects the medicalentities to EntityMention and the Page nodes. As we mentioned earlier, we keptboth the EntityMention and the disambiguated MedicalEntity in the graph toimprove flexibility in representing data.

7.6.4 Processing, loading, and mapping ontologies
In this phase, we load UMLS, SNOMED, and HPO ontologies into the KG. TheUMLS serves as the entry point to access specific information across multipleontologies. For this reason, we first load the SNOMED and HPO ontologies andthen map each entity from them to UMLS.
INGESTING SNOMED
The following listing creates nodes and relationships in Neo4j fromsct2_Relationship_Full_US1000124_20220901.txt.

Listing 7.14 Ingesting SNOMED: loading relationships
[...] 
class SnomedRelationshipsImporter(BaseImporter): #1 
  [...]   
  def set_constraints(self):  #2 
    queries = [ 
        ( 
            "CREATE CONSTRAINT IF NOT EXISTS FOR (n:SnomedEntity) " 
            "REQUIRE n.id IS UNIQUE" 
        ), 
        ( 
            "CREATE INDEX snomedNodeName IF NOT EXISTS " 
            "FOR (n:SnomedEntity) ON (n.name)" 
        ), 
        ( 
            "CREATE INDEX snomedRelationId IF NOT EXISTS " 
            "FOR ()-[r:SNOMED_RELATION]-() ON (r.id)" 
        ), 
        ( 
            "CREATE INDEX snomedRelationType IF NOT EXISTS " 
            "FOR ()-[r:SNOMED_RELATION]-() ON (r.type)" 
        ), 
        ( 
            "CREATE INDEX snomedRelationUmls IF NOT EXISTS " 
            "FOR ()-[r:SNOMED_RELATION]-() ON (r.umls)" 
        ), 
    ] 
 
 
    for q in queries: 
      self.connection.query(q, db=self.db) 
 
  def import_snomed_rels(self): #3 
    query = """ 
       UNWIND $batch as item 
       MERGE (e1:SnomedEntity {id: item.sourceId}) 
       MERGE (e2:SnomedEntity {id: item.destinationId}) 
       MERGE (e1)-[:SNOMED_RELATION {id: item.typeId}]->(e2) 
       FOREACH(ignoreMe IN CASE WHEN item.typeId = '116680003'  
       ↪ THEN [true] ELSE [] END| 
         MERGE (e1)-[:SNOMED_IS_A]->(e2)  #4 
       ) 
       """ 
 
size = self.get_csv_size(snomedRels_file)  #5 

self.batch_store(snomed_rels_query, self.get_rows(snomedRels_file), 
↪ size=size) #6
#1 Extends the BaseImporter class, which contains the base importing functionalities #2 Defines constraints and indexes on SNOMED entities and properties #3 Imports SNOMED relationships using a parametric query #4 Creates the SNOMED_IS_A relationship type to track hierarchical connections between entities #5 Gets the size of the file (default implementation in the BaseImporter class) #6 Loads the SNOMED data in batches (implementation in the BaseImporter class) 
SNOMED includes hundreds of relationships. To keep the graph schema as simpleas possible, we decided to create a unique SNOMED_RELATION, and we store therelationship name as a type property. In listing 7.14 we create a SNOMED_IS_A
relationship to define the hierarchical connections; we will see shortly why thischoice is handy to propagate information from the root to the leaf nodes.
Now that we have ingested the nodes and relationships to shape the graph, weneed to enrich this structure by adding names and aliases. The following classextracts information from sct2_Description_Full-en_US1000124_20220901.txt.

Listing 7.15 Ingesting SNOMED: loading names and aliases
[...] 
class SnomedNamesImporter(BaseImporter): 
  [...] 
 
  def import_snomed_names(self, snomedNames_file): 
        snomed_names_concepts_query = """ 
        UNWIND $batch as item 
        MATCH (e1:SnomedEntity) 
        -[r:SNOMED_RELATION {id: item.conceptId}]-> 
        (e2:SnomedEntity) 
        WHERE item.conceptId <> '116680003' AND r.id = item.conceptId  
        SET r.type = CASE  
                WHEN r.type IS NULL THEN item.termAsType 
                ELSE r.type END,  #1 
            r.aliases = CASE  
                WHEN item.termAsType IN r.aliases THEN r.aliases 
                ELSE coalesce(r.aliases,[]) + item.termAsType END  #2 
        """ 
 
        snomed_names_entities_query = """ 
        UNWIND $batch as item 
        MATCH (e:SnomedEntity {id: item.conceptId}) 
        SET e.name = CASE  
                WHEN e.name IS NULL THEN item.term 
                ELSE e.name END,  #3 
            e.aliases = CASE  
                WHEN item.term in e.aliases THEN  e.aliases 
                ELSE coalesce(e.aliases, []) + item.term END  #4 
        """ 
        size = self.get_csv_size(snomedNames_file) 
        self.batch_store( 
          snomed_names_concepts_query, 
          self.get_rows(snomedNames_file), 
         size=size) 
        self.batch_store( 
          snomed_names_entities_query, 
          self.get_rows(snomedNames_file), 
          size=size) 
 
[...]
#1 Adds the relationship name in the type property #2 Adds relationship aliases #3 Adds the node name #4 Adds node aliases 

This class adds names and aliases to the nodes and relationships loaded into thegraph. The next step involves propagating information from the root nodes to allsubnodes, down to the leaf nodes. The first-level nodes represent the archetypalentities of SNOMED in the medical domain, such as diseases, body structures,substances, and events. These root nodes define the semantic types of the entitiesavailable in SNOMED. However, this information is implicit in the data weingested because for each other entity, there are only names and aliases in theoriginal data. Therefore, we need a mechanism to transfer this information throughthe ontology’s tree structure; this way, we can easily detect that a deep entity is adisease or a product. Figure 7.11 clarifies this propagation mechanism.

Figure 7.11 A sample of the hierarchical structure of the SNOMED ontology. Using this hierarchicalstructure, nodes located on a deeper level, such as Ecallantide and Retinopathy associated with AIDS, canbe categorized using the information from the first-level nodes, such as Pharmaceutical product andDisease, which represent the archetypal entities of the ontology.
The next listing retrieves all nodes, following the hierarchical structure topropagate information from first-level nodes to deeper nodes.

Listing 7.16 Ingesting SNOMED: propagating labels from first-level nodes
[...] 
class SnomedLabelPropagator():     
[...]   
 
  def get_rows(self): 
    propagation_query = """ 
      MATCH p=(n:SnomedEntity)<-[:SNOMED_IS_A]-(m:SnomedEntity)  
      WHERE n.id= "138875005" // Root node 
      WITH distinct m as first_node 
 
      CALL apoc.path.expandConfig(first_node, { #1 
              relationshipFilter: '<SNOMED_IS_A', 
                minLevel: 1, 
                maxLevel: -1, 
                uniqueness: 'RELATIONSHIP_GLOBAL' 
            }) yield path 
 
     UNWIND nodes(path) as other_level  #2 
     WITH first_node, collect(DISTINCT other_level) as uniques 
             UNWIND uniques as unique_other_level 
             WITH first_node,unique_other_level 
             WHERE not first_node.name in coalesce(unique_other_level.typ
e,[]) 
 
             RETURN unique_other_level.id as id, first_node.name as label 
- #3 
            """ 
 
   with self._driver.session(database=self._database) as session: 
     result = session.run(query=propagation_query) 
     for record in iter(result): 
        yield dict(record) 
[...]
#1 Uses expandConfig to set the rules for traversing the hierarchy #2 Gets the nodes resulting from this traversal process #3 Returns all the nodes characterized by a specific type 
The SNOMED_IS_A relationship propagates the semantic types through the treestructure by using the hierarchical connections between entities.
INGESTING HPO

The following listings outline the primary steps for ingesting the HPO ontology.More details, including the creation of the proper indices, are discussed in chapter3 and included in the Cypher code in the book’s repository. First we import theHPO ontology using the Neosemantics plugin.
Listing 7.17 Ingesting HPO: loading the ontology
CALL n10s.rdf.import.fetch("http://purl.obolibrary.org/obo/hp.owl","RDF/X
ML");
The HPO ontology is available in the RDF/XML format, and it is converted into aNeo4j graph structure to be processed using Cypher.
Next, we add the HPO label to nodes representing phenotypic feature entities.
Listing 7.18 Ingesting HPO: adding the HpoEntity label to phenotypic features
MATCH (n:Resource) 
WHERE n.uri STARTS WITH "http://purl.obolibrary.org/obo/HP" 
SET n:HpoEntity, 
 n.id = coalesce(n.id, replace(apoc.text.replace(n.uri,'(.*)ob
o/',''),'_', ':'));
Now we need to process the annotation file that describes the connections betweenthe phenotypic features and diseases. To make this step more efficient, we use thefollowing query to load the disease entities as graph nodes.
Listing 7.19 Ingesting HPO: creating HpoDiseaseEntity nodes
LOAD CSV FROM 'https://github.com/obophenotype/human-phenotype- 
↪ ontology/releases/latest/download/phenotype.hpoa' AS row 
FIELDTERMINATOR '\t' 
WITH row 
SKIP 5 
MERGE (dis:Resource:HpoDiseaseEntity {id: row[0]}) 
ON CREATE SET dis.label = row[1];
The next step is to create the relations between the available phenotypic featuresand disease nodes.

Listing 7.20 Ingesting HPO: relations between HpoEntity and HpoDiseaseEntity
LOAD CSV FROM 'https://github.com/obophenotype/human-phenotype-ontology/ 
↪ releases/latest/download/phenotype.hpoa' AS row 
FIELDTERMINATOR '\t' 
WITH row 
SKIP 5 
MATCH (dis:HpoDiseaseEntity) 
WHERE dis.id = row[0] 
MATCH (phe:HpoEntity) 
WHERE phe.id = row[3] 
MERGE (dis)-[:HAS_PHENOTYPIC_FEATURE]->(phe)
The following query establishes the connection between the disambiguated entitiesextracted from the text and the ontology nodes.
Listing 7.21 Integrating SNOMED through the UMLS
MATCH (m:MedicalEntity) 
WITH m 
MATCH (d:SnomedEntity) 
WHERE m.id in d.umls_ids 
WITH m, d 
MERGE (m)-[:IS_SNOMED_ENTITY]->(d)
We perform an analogous process for the HPO ontology (see the full code formore details). The next query connects MedicalEntity nodes and the
HpoDiseaseEntity nodes from the HPO annotation file.
Listing 7.22 Connecting MedicalEntity and HpoDiseaseEntity nodes
MATCH (m:MedicalEntity) 
WITH m 
MATCH (d:HpoDiseaseEntity) 
WHERE m.id in d.umls_ids  
WITH m, d 
MERGE (m)-[:IS_DISEASE_ENTITY]->(d)
In the next section, we generate the co-occurrence relationship between entitieslocated in the same sentence.
7.6.5 Generating entity co-occurrences
Identifying co-occurrences of medical entities in the text is a fundamental step inenabling advanced use cases that combine unstructured knowledge from textual

content with structured knowledge in domain ontologies. The query in listing 7.23creates a new relationship called COOCCURR between medical entities identified inthe same sentence.
DEFINITION  Co-occurrence refers to the projection of Page nodes onto
Entity nodes.
Listing 7.23 Creating co-occurrence relationships at the sentence level
CALL apoc.periodic.iterate( 
  "MATCH (n:Page) WHERE exists( (n)-[:MENTIONS_ENTITY]->(:MedicalEntity) 
) 
  RETURN n",  
  "MATCH (n)-[r:MENTIONS_ENTITY]->(m:MedicalEntity) 
  WITH n, r.sentence_index as sentences, m  
  UNWIND sentences as sentence 
  WITH n, sentence, collect(distinct m) as entities 
 
  UNWIND range(0, size(entities)-2) as i 
  UNWIND range(i+1, size(entities)-1) as j 
 
  WITH n, sentence, entities, i, j 
  MATCH (m1) WHERE id(m1) = id(entities[i]) 
  MATCH (m2) WHERE id(m2) = id(entities[j]) 
 
  WITH n, sentence, entities, i, j, m1, m2 
  MERGE (m1)-[s:COOCCURR]-(m2) 
  ON CREATE SET s.count = 1,  
       s.sentences = [sentence] 
  ON MATCH SET s.count = s.count + 1,  
   s.sentences = s.sentences + sentence",  
{batchSize: 50})
This query produces more than 25,000 relationships in the KG, making explicit theconnections between medical entities located in the same sentence. As we willdiscuss next, analyzing the ontology connections between co-occurring entities letsus discover the established knowledge related to these entities and uncover newinformation that is not yet established in biomedical ontologies.
7.7 KG-based use cases
In this section, code examples will show how we handle the following use casesusing KGs in combination with NED:

Conceptual search
Structured knowledge-based search
KG-based interpretability and discovery
Uncovering new knowledge
Figure 7.12 includes the analysis step related to the use cases defined in thisapplication domain.

Figure 7.12 After generating the KG, we can perform analyses by applying defined use cases to addressbusiness problems and provide solutions based on the KG.
NOTE  Your query results may vary slightly from those shown in thechapter due to differences in environments, Neo4j indexing behavior, datapipeline ingestion order, and the nondeterministic aspects of entity extractionperformed by scispaCy.
7.7.1 Conceptual search

Conceptual search is related to the capacity to reconcile—and return to the user—different expressions with the same meaning or distinguish similar terms that referto distinct entities. Performing a conceptual search can help us expand or focus thesearch for specific documents and the related portions of text that mention theentity. Figure 7.13 provides a high-level comparison of conceptual search andtraditional full-text search.
Figure 7.13 Differences between traditional full-text search and conceptual search. The full-text searchquery is performed directly on the set of documents, whereas the conceptual search query usesinformation from ontologies to expand the search space before searching the documents.

Let’s examine the effect of conceptual search starting from a traditional full-textsearch. The following search query tries to retrieve all documents mentioning“breakbone fever.”
Listing 7.24 Full-text search query with “breakbone fever” as the input string
CALL db.index.fulltext.queryNodes("PageText", "breakbone fever") 
YIELD node, score 
WITH node as p, score as score 
MATCH (f:File)-[:CONTAINS_PAGE]->(p) 
RETURN f.id as `File ID␀, p.page_idx as `Page index`, score as Score 
LIMIT 5
Table 7.1 shows the results of the full-text search ordered by score value. The firstcolumn lists the document path, the second column shows the page index in thedocument, and the third column reports the score computed by the full-text searchalgorithm.
Table 7.1 The top five pages retrieved by a full-text search for “breakbone fever”
File ID Pageindex Score
sample_dataset-PublicUse/ECDC Documents/west nile virus/emerging-vector-borne-diseases_annual-epidemiological-report-2014.pdf 5 2.12 
sample_dataset-PublicUse/ECDC Documents/west nile virus/emerging-vector-borne-diseases_annual-epidemiological-report-2014.pdf 4 2.09 
sample_dataset-PublicUse/ECDC Documents/zika virus/Communicable-disease-threats-report-26-mar-2016.pdf 10 2.08 
sample_dataset-PublicUse/ECDC Documents/ebola/communicable-disease-threats-report-13-19-mar-2016.pdf 9 2.08 
sample_dataset-PublicUse/ECDC Documents/zika virus/Communicable-disease-threats-report-26-mar-2016.pdf 10 2.08 
This type of search identifies keywords in a set of documents by using fuzzy logic.In this case, “breakbone” is never mentioned in the text, but the term “fever”appears multiple times in the high-scored documents. Nevertheless, we areinterested in identifying documents that mention this specific disease or,eventually, the causative agent of this disease.
In the UMLS knowledge base, the code C0011311 identifies this entity, which canappear in various forms, including “dengue fever,” “dungero,” and “dandy fever.”So, we next run the following query to retrieve all medical entities identified bythe scispaCy model whose alias is “breakbone fever.”

Listing 7.25 Finding mentions of the entity whose alias is “breakbone fever”
MATCH (f:File)-[:CONTAINS_PAGE]->(p) 
      -[r:MENTIONS_MENTION]->(m)-[:DISAMBIGUATED_TO]->(e) 
WHERE "breakbone fever" IN [x IN e.aliases | toLower(x)]  #1 
 
 
 
UNWIND range(0, size(r.start_chars) - 1) AS mention  #2 
WITH f, p, e, m, r, mention 
RETURN DISTINCT 
  f.id AS `File ID␀, 
  p.page_idx AS `Page index`, 
  apoc.text.join( 
    collect( 
      substring( 
        p.text, 
        apoc.coll.max([r.start_chars[mention] - 100, 0]),  #3 
        r.end_chars[mention] - r.start_chars[mention] + 200  #4 
      ) 
    )[0..3],  #5 
    '\n\n' 
  ) AS `Mention contexts`, 
  size(collect(m.name)) AS `Number of mentions` 
ORDER BY `Number of mentions` DESC 
LIMIT 5
#1 Filters nodes by checking if the alias "breakbone fever" (in lowercase) exists among aliases of theentity #2 Iterates over each mention index in the list of start characters to handle multiple mentions per page #3 Calculates a starting index for the substring, ensuring that it doesn't go below zero by subtracting100 from the start position #4 Determines the length of the text snippet by computing the difference between the end and start ofthe mention and adding 200 for extra context #5 Limits the collected context snippets to the first three for each file–page combination to keep theoutput concise

Comparing the results with those from the full-text search, we see that the mostrelevant pages are completely different. Let’s try to update the conceptual searchquery to show and explore the full result set (remove the LIMIT clause). The firstresult from the full-text query is located at the 19th position in the conceptualsearch query. This specific document has 17 mentions of the UMLS entity,whereas the top-scored result of the conceptual search query includes 22 mentionsof the C0011311 UMLS entity.
Adopting conceptual search has a huge effect on our application domain. We canretrieve more precise and detailed information compared to the full-text search: inaddition to the document path and the page index, we can identify the portion oftext that mentions the entity and the number of occurrences of this entity on thepage. Thus, conceptual search enables other features that improve theexplainability of the retrieved document. Because the NED model lets us identifythe position of the detected entity in the text, we can eventually perform precisedebugging tests to identify the cases in which the model did not perform asexpected.

Conceptual search also enhances the search process in scenarios where a word orexpression has different meanings based on context. For example, the word“islands” has a traditional meaning, but it takes on a completely different semanticcontext when used in the expression “islands of Langerhans.” A traditional full-text search might lead to irrelevant results referring to land masses surrounded bywater. By using the conceptual search mechanism, we can filter out these resultsand broaden the search scope to include other expressions, such as “pancreaticislets,” to capture more relevant content. As we discuss next, the core concept ofconceptual search can be expanded by linking pages that include medical entitiesconnected through ontology relationships.
7.7.2 Structured knowledge-based search
Using structured knowledge-based search, we can retrieve information from textby using formalized knowledge organized in domain ontologies and createnontrivial relationships between different pieces of text across multiple documents.We’ve already seen how we can aggregate information referring to the sameconcept, such as dengue fever or pancreatic islets, regardless of ambiguous ormultiple names. However, by using the knowledge embedded in ontologies likeSNOMED, we can aggregate and connect unstructured content driven by ontologyrelationships. For instance, given the importance of donations of cells like theislets of Langerhans, it would be beneficial to aggregate all text that mentionsdiseases that can affect these cells and thus compromise the donation process.Figure 7.14 shows a mental model of the difference between a conceptual searchquery and a structured knowledge-based query.

Figure 7.14 Differences between conceptual search and structured knowledge-based search. In this case,the search process involves medical entities connected by ontology relationships to the entity detected inthe search query. Starting from the “islets of Langerhans” search, the system searches for “diabetestype 1” and “hyperglycaemia,” which are two diseases that can affect the islets of Langerhans.
The following query retrieves portions of text that mention diseases that can affectthe islets of Langerhans.

Listing 7.26 Getting text about diseases that can affect the islets of Langerhans
MATCH (m1:MedicalEntity)-[:IS_SNOMED_ENTITY]->(s1:SnomedEntity) 
<-[r1:SNOMED_RELATION]-(s2:SnomedEntity) 
<-[:IS_SNOMED_ENTITY]-(e:MedicalEntity) 
WHERE m1.name = "Islets of Langerhans" AND r1.type = "FINDING_SITE"  #1 
WITH e 
MATCH path = (f:File)-[:CONTAINS_PAGE]->(p) 
-[r:MENTIONS_MENTION]->(m)-[:DISAMBIGUATED_TO]->(e) 
UNWIND range(0, size(r.start_chars) - 1) AS mention  #2 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
WITH f, p, r, e, mention, 
     apoc.coll.max([r.start_chars[mention] - 100, 0]) AS start,  #3 
     apoc.coll.min([r.end_chars[mention] + 100, size(p.text)]) AS end  #4 
WITH f, p, r, e, mention, substring(p.text, start, end - start) AS contex
t  #5 
WITH f, p, 
     collect(DISTINCT e.name) AS `Mentioned entities`,  #6 
     collect(context)[0..3] AS contexts  #7 
RETURN DISTINCT 
  f.id AS `File ID␀, 
  p.page_idx AS `Page index`, 
  `Mentioned entities`, 
  apoc.text.join(contexts, '\n\n') AS `Mention contexts` 
ORDER BY size(`Mentioned entities`) DESC 
LIMIT 5
#1 Filters for SNOMED entities related to "Islets of Langerhans" by the FINDING_SITE relationshiptype #2 Iterates over each mention instance using indices from start_chars, allowing multiple mentions perrelation #3 Computes a start index for context extraction, backing up 100 characters without going below 0 #4 Calculates an end index up to 100 characters beyond the mention without exceeding the page textlength #5 Extracts a substring of the page text from the calculated start to end position as the context window #6 Gathers a deduplicated list of medical entity names mentioned on the page #7 Limits the collected context windows to the first three mentions

In listing 7.26, we extend the logic of the conceptual search query, taking acollection of entities from the ontology as input and retrieving the related details inthe documents. One of the most interesting results is from page 144 of Guide tothe Quality and Safety of Organs for Transplantation, 7th ed., reported in column4 of table 7.3. This page mentions Hyperglycemia, which is explicitly connected tothe Islets of Langerhans entity through the FINDING_SITE relationship, in thecontext of managing a potential donor who has suffered head trauma. Thissentence is located in a section dedicated to pancreas donation focused on donor-maintenance protocols. This critical information would not have been retrievedthrough the conceptual search mechanism. The other results mention different formsof diabetes mellitus, which is particularly relevant in the donation of pancreaticislets.
A structured knowledge-based search can also be performed by using the longestpaths in an ontology. Let’s consider the Zika virus example. This virus can becategorized as a Togavirus, and it is transmitted to humans via species ofarthropods that feed on blood, especially insects and arachnids. Suppose we areinterested in all diseases mentioned in the document that are caused by aTogavirus. We can explore a path that concatenates multiple CAUSATIVE_AGENT
relationships in the SNOMED ontology, using the results to acquire the desireddocuments; figure 7.15 shows an example.

Figure 7.15 SNOMED ontology paths including only the CAUSATIVE_AGENT relationship. Navigating thissubset of relationships is particularly useful for identifying diseases carried by the same virus types.
We can expand the search to involve entities such as Yellow fever, Rift valley fever,and Rubella that do not have a direct connection with the entity specified in thesearch query (Zika virus). Listing 7.27 shows the query to use these complex pathsfor retrieving relevant documents. This example is particularly exciting for ourapplication domain because we can retrieve documents mentioning similardiseases based on the type of virus they have in common.

Listing 7.27 Getting documents mentioning diseases caused by Togaviruses
MATCH (m1:MedicalEntity)-[:IS_SNOMED_ENTITY]->(s1:SnomedEntity) 
-[r1:SNOMED_RELATION*3..3]-(s2:SnomedEntity) 
      <-[:IS_SNOMED_ENTITY]-(e:MedicalEntity)  #1 
WHERE m1.name = "Zika Virus"  
 
AND all(x IN r1 WHERE x.type = "CAUSATIVE_AGENT")  #2 
WITH DISTINCT e 
 
MATCH path = (f:File)-[:CONTAINS_PAGE]->(p) 
-[r:MENTIONS_MENTION]->(m)-[:DISAMBIGUATED_TO]->(e) 
WITH f, e, collect(p.page_idx) AS pages_list  #3 
RETURN DISTINCT 
  f.id AS `File ID␀, 
  pages_list, 
  collect(DISTINCT e.name) AS `Mentioned entity` 
ORDER BY size(`Mentioned entity`) DESC 
LIMIT 5
#1 Traverses three SNOMED_RELATION hops to discover indirectly related medical entities #2 Filters paths where all three relationships are CAUSATIVE_AGENT, to ensure semantic consistency #3 Collects indices from all pages in which the entity is mentioned

7.7.3 KG-based interpretability and discovery
Starting from the co-occurrence of entities in the same sentence, KG-basedinterpretability and discovery lets us analyze how these entities are connected inthe ontologies and what the nature of this connection is. In some cases, theontology connections reflect the reason for the co-occurring entities in a specificsentence (interpretability). This analysis can also validate co-occurring entitiesagainst an ontology. And other cases, ontology connections add knowledge thatexpands the information provided by the sentence (discovery).
To better understand the value of this use case, consider listing 7.28, whichincludes sentences from the document entitled “Proposal for a Directive of theEuropean Parliament and of the Council Setting Standards of Quality and Safetyfor the Collection, Testing, Processing, Storage, and Distribution of Human Bloodand Blood Components and Amending Council Directive 89/381/EEC.” In thisdocument, “AIDS” and “Hepatitis” co-occur two times.
Listing 7.28 Sentences where AIDS and Hepatitis co-occur
SENTENCE 1: The reasons why they should not donate which put recipients a
t  
risk, such as unsafe sexual behaviour, HIV/ AIDS, hepatitis, drug  
addiction and the use and abuse of drugs; 
 
[...] 
 
SENTENCE 2: Infectious diseases persons suffering or having suffered from 
- Babesiosis 
- Hepatitis B (HBsAg confirmed positive) 
- Hepatitis C 
- Hepatitis, infectious (of unexplained aetiology) 
- HIV/AIDS
“AIDS” and “Hepatitis” appear close to each other in these sentences because theyboth represent a risk factor in the donation process: they are infectious diseases.This information is directly encoded in SNOMED, and expressed by differentontology paths. The following listing shows a subset.

Listing 7.29 Paths connecting entities, interpretability perspective
(AIDS)-[:PATHOLOGICAL_PROCESS]->(Infectious disease) 
<-[:DUE_TO]-(Hepatitis due to infection) 
-[:IS_A]->(Inflammatory disorder of liver) 
 
(AIDS)-[:PATHOLOGICAL_PROCESS]->(Infectious disease) 
<-[:DUE_TO]-(Viral hepatitis) 
-[:IS_A]->(Inflammatory disorder of liver)
These ontology paths define connections between these two entities and encodethe meaning of the co-occurrence of “AIDS” and “Hepatitis” (which is labeled“Inflammatory disorder of liver” in the SNOMED ontology). We also validate theextracted entities against the ontology, which enables us to understand why theseentities were extracted in the same sentence.
Other types of SNOMED paths reveal interesting connections between AIDS andhepatitis. For example, the first SNOMED path in the next listing shows that AIDSis related to a disorder defined as “Hepatomegaly associated with AIDS” thataffects the liver. The second entry reports that a specific form of hepatitis called“Lupus hepatitis” involves the immune system as “AIDS.”
Listing 7.30 Paths connecting entities, discovery perspective
(AIDS)<-[:ASSOCIATED_WITH]-(Hepatomegaly associated with AIDS (disorder)) 
-[:FINDING_SITE]->(Liver) 
<-[:FINDING_SITE]-(Inflammatory disorder of liver) 
 
(AIDS)-[:HAS_DEFINITIONAL_MANIFESTATION]->(Immune system finding) 
<-[:HAS_DEFINITIONAL_MANIFESTATION]-(Lupus hepatitis) 
-[:IS_A]->(Inflammatory disorder of liver)
The ontology supports us in understanding why a pair of medical entities appear inthe sentence and lets us discover new details related to this pair. Figure 7.16illustrates integrating domain ontologies into a KG built from natural languagecontent; it shows “Dengue” and “Zika virus” as examples of co-occurrence.

Figure 7.16 Mental model describing the KG-based interpretability and discovery process. Co-occurring entities in the text can be connected by multiple paths in the SNOMED ontology.
Let’s dive into the details and see how to apply practical solutions in the SoHOdomain to enable interpretability and discovery with a real KG. The followinglisting retrieves the top five entity types that co-occur with “Zika virus.”

Listing 7.31 Retrieving the top entity types co-occurring with “Zika virus”
MATCH (m1:MedicalEntity)-[r:COOCCURR]-(m2:MedicalEntity) 
WHERE m1.id= "C0318793" 
RETURN m2.type as `Entity Type`, count(m2.type) as `Number of co-occurren
ces`  
ORDER BY count(m2.type) DESC 
LIMIT 5
This query computes the number of co-occurring entity types to identify the mostrelevant ones. The results are shown in table 7.5.
Table 7.5 Top entity types co-occurring with “Zika virus”
Entity Number of co-occurrences
Geographic Area 255 
Qualitative Concept 132 
Disease or Syndrome 125 
Functional Concept 106 
Finding 98 
Most of the results include Geographic Area. This is related to the fact that “Zikavirus” is often mentioned in bulletins that report the spread of communicablediseases. Other categories, such as Qualitative Concept and Functional
Concept, include broader concepts that in most cases are not relevant for ourexample. For this reason, we will focus on the co-occurring Disease or Syndrome
entities. The next query finds co-occurring entities and the portion of text fromwhich this co-occurrence was extracted.

Listing 7.32 Getting co-occurring disease entities with context
MATCH (n1:MedicalEntity)-[r:COOCCURR]-(n2:MedicalEntity) 
WHERE n1.id = "C0318793" AND n2.type = "Disease or Syndrome"  #1 
WITH n1, r, n2 
ORDER BY r.count DESC 
MATCH (f:File)-[:CONTAINS_PAGE]->(p:Page) 
      -[r1:MENTIONS_MENTION]->(m1)-[:DISAMBIGUATED_TO]->(n1), 
      (p)-[r2:MENTIONS_MENTION]->(m2)-[:DISAMBIGUATED_TO]->(n2) 
WHERE r1.sentence_index = r2.sentence_index  #2 
WITH f, p, r1, r2, n2 
RETURN DISTINCT 
  f.id AS `File ID␀, 
  p.page_idx AS `Page index`, 
  n2.id AS `Co-occurring entity id`, 
  n2.name AS `Co-occurring entity name`, 
  CASE 
    WHEN r1.end_chars[0] > r2.start_chars[0] 
    THEN substring(p.text, r2.start_chars[0],  
    ↪ r1.end_chars[0] - r2.start_chars[0])  #3 
    ELSE substring(p.text, r1.start_chars[0],  
    ↪ r2.end_chars[0] - r1.start_chars[0])  #4 
  END AS `Mentions context`
#1 Filters for entities co-occurring with "C0318793" (Zika virus) and restricts to those of type "Diseaseor Syndrome" #2 Ensures that both entities were mentioned in the same sentence on the page #3 Captures the co-occurrence span #4 Ensures that the context window always runs from the earlier to the later character position

The entities Zika virus and Communicable Diseases (UMLS ID C0009450) occurmany times in the same sentence. This is because many of the ingested bulletinshave a similar structure, such as “COMMUNICABLE DISEASE THREATSREPORT Zika: No mosquito-borne Zika virus […].” However, other co-occurrence examples are more relevant for interpretability and discovery. Forinstance, Zika virus often co-occurs with the following entities: Zika VirusInfection (UMLS ID C0276289), Dengue Fever (UMLS ID C0011311), andChikungunya Fever (UMLS ID C0008055).

The co-occurrence with Zika Virus Infection is understandable. However, thesemantic connection between these two entities is directly available in theSNOMED ontology. The following query uses the corresponding SNOMED IDsand labels to show the SNOMED connection between Zika virus disease(SNOMED ID 3928002) and Zika virus (SNOMED ID 50471002).
Listing 7.33 Getting paths between Zika virus disease and Zika virus
MATCH (s1), (s2) 
WHERE s1.id = "3928002" AND s2.id = "50471002" 
WITH s1, s2, allShortestPaths((s1)-[:SNOMED_RELATION*1..8]-(s2)) AS paths  
#1 
UNWIND paths AS path 
WITH relationships(path) AS path_edges, 
     nodes(path) AS path_nodes 
WITH  
  [n IN path_nodes | n.name] AS node_names, 
  [r IN path_edges | COALESCE(r.type, 'IS_A')] AS rel_types,  #2 
  [n IN path_edges | startnode(n).name] AS rel_starts  #3 
WITH [i IN range(0, size(node_names) - 1) | 
  CASE 
    WHEN i = size(node_names) - 1 
    THEN '(' + node_names[i] + ')'  #4 
    WHEN node_names[i] = rel_starts[i] 
    THEN '(' + node_names[i] + ')' + '-[:' + rel_types[i] + ']->'  #5 
    ELSE '(' + node_names[i] + ')' + '<-[:' + rel_types[i] + ']-'  #6 
  END 
] AS string_paths 
RETURN DISTINCT apoc.text.join(string_paths, '') AS `Extracted paths`
#1 Finds shortest paths (up to eight hops) between two SNOMED concepts usingSNOMED_RELATION #2 Uses the relationship type (default "IS_A") to ensure valid labeling #3 Retrieves the name of the starting node for each relationship to determine the relationship direction #4 Completes the path string #5 Indicates that the relationship is outgoing from the current node #6 Indicates that the relationship is incoming to the current node 
This query returns all the shortest paths between Zika virus and Zika virus diseasein a pretty-printed format. The result is shown next.
Listing 7.34 Paths connecting Zika virus disease and Zika virus
(Zika virus disease)-[:CAUSATIVE_AGENT]->(Zika virus)
In this case, the SNOMED ontology provides a relationship that clearly“interprets” the meaning of this co-occurrence. Such a connection reflects the

linguistic and conceptual proximity of the disease and its causative agent inclinical and epidemiological texts. In our scenario, we provide graph-basedaugmented information, which makes explicit why these co-occurring entities canbe validated.
As reported in table 7.6, the Zika virus medical entity also co-occurs with anotherdisease, Dengue Fever. We can explore the ontology paths connecting these twoentities by running the query in listing 7.33 and replacing the WHERE clause with
s1.id="38362002" AND s2.id="50471002". The results are as follows.

<-[:IS_A]-(Zika virus disease)-[:CAUSATIVE_AGENT]->(Zika virus) 
 
(Dengue)-[:IS_A]->(Mosquito-borne flavivirus fever) 
<-[:IS_A]-(Zika virus disease)-[:CAUSATIVE_AGENT]->(Zika virus) 
 
(Dengue)-[:IS_A]->(Viral disease) 
<-[:IS_A]-(Zika virus disease)-[:CAUSATIVE_AGENT]->(Zika virus) 
 
(Dengue)-[:PATHOLOGICAL_PROCESS_(ATTRIBUTE)]->(Infectious process  
↪ (qualifier value)) 
<-[:PATHOLOGICAL_PROCESS_(ATTRIBUTE)]-(Congenital Zika virus infection) 
-[:CAUSATIVE_AGENT]->(Zika virus)  
 
(Dengue)-[:CAUSATIVE_AGENT]->(Arthropod-borne organism) 
<-[:CAUSATIVE_AGENT]-(Zika virus disease) 
-[:CAUSATIVE_AGENT]->(Zika virus)

↪ (qualifier value)) 
<-[:PATHOLOGICAL_PROCESS_(ATTRIBUTE)]-(Zika virus disease) 
-[:CAUSATIVE_AGENT]->(Zika virus)

Multiple paths connect Dengue and Zika virus, including key entities such as Viraldisease and Infectious disease that allow us to interpret why these diseases co-

occur in the same sentence (see the last row of table 7.6). In addition, entities suchas Disease due to Flavivirus, Togavirus, and Mosquito-borne flavivirus feverprovide insights into how Dengue and Zika virus are connected, regardless of thesentence in which they are mentioned.
This validation process can be extended to other biomedical ontologies, includingthe HPO. For example, the results of the following query demonstrate how co-occurrence patterns between phenotypic features (e.g., Renal cell carcinoma,Leukemia) and associated disease entities (e.g., von Hippel-Lindau syndrome,Colorectal cancer, RETINOBLASTOMA) can be systematically extracted andvalidated. This approach enables the identification of clinically relevantphenotype–disease associations grounded in document-level evidence.
Listing 7.36 Finding HPO disease entities that co-occur with phenotypic features
MATCH (d:HpoDiseaseEntity)<-[:IS_DISEASE_ENTITY]-(n1:MedicalEntity) 
      -[r:COOCCURR]-(n2:MedicalEntity)-[:IS_HPO_ENTITY]->(h:HpoEntity) 
WHERE EXISTS((d)-[:HAS_PHENOTYPIC_FEATURE]->(h)) 
 AND n2.id in ["C0007134", "C0376545"]  #1 
WITH n1, n2, d, h 
 
MATCH (f:File)-[:CONTAINS_PAGE]->(p:Page) 
      -[r1:MENTIONS_MENTION]->(m1)-[:DISAMBIGUATED_TO]->(n1), 
      (p)-[r2:MENTIONS_MENTION]->(m2)-[:DISAMBIGUATED_TO]->(n2) 
WHERE r1.sentence_index = r2.sentence_index  #2 
WITH f, p, r1, r2, n1, n2, d, h 
 
RETURN DISTINCT 
  f.id AS `File name`, 
  p.page_idx AS `Page index`, 
  h.label AS `HpoEntity name`, 
  d.label AS `HpoDiseaseEntity name`, 
  CASE 
    WHEN r1.end_chars[0] > r2.start_chars[0] 
    THEN substring(p.text, r2.start_chars[0], r1.end_chars[0]  
    - r2.start_chars[0])  #3 
    ELSE substring(p.text, r1.start_chars[0], r2.end_chars[0]  
    - r1.start_chars[0])  #4 
  END AS `Mentions context`
#1 Selects pairs of medical entities where n1 co-occurs with a fixed subset of phenotype entities and islinked to a disease d that has the phenotype h #2 Filters the results to mentions that appear in the same sentence #3 Extracts the surrounding text to form a co-occurrence snippet #4 Ensures the correct ordering for text extraction 

Unlike earlier examples, here we specify that one medical entity must be a diseaseand the other a phenotypic feature indexed in the HPO annotation file. The resultsof this query are listed in table 7.7.

This use case has practical applications for analysts, who can derive interestingpatterns from co-occurring entity types. For example, in the case of multiple co-occurring diseases, we can verify which ontology paths connect these diseases. Onthe other hand, the absence of interesting paths between co-occurring entitiessignals new knowledge that is not encoded in biomedical ontologies; we discussthis case next.
7.7.4 Uncovering new knowledge

In a context that changes quickly due to research advancements, some knowledgein the text has not yet been consolidated in medical ontologies. As a consequence,entities that co-occur in the same sentence may not have a direct match in terms ofinterpretability and discovery in the domain ontologies.
Instead of using the ontology to enrich the information of the KG, we can use aKG built from textual content to suggest new facts that can be integrated into theontology. This use case allows us to identify new patterns in the text that can beuseful in the medical domain. To identify this type of pattern, let’s recap thediseases that co-occur most with Zika virus by running the following query.
Listing 7.37 Finding the top diseases co-occurring with “Zika virus” in text
MATCH (n1:MedicalEntity)-[r:COOCCURR]-(n2:MedicalEntity) 
WHERE n1.id= "C0318793" and n2.type = "Disease or Syndrome" 
RETURN n2.name, r.count 
ORDER BY r.count DESC 
LIMIT 5
The results are shown in table 7.8.
Table 7.8 Top diseases co-occurring with Zika virus
Disease entity Occurrences
Communicable Diseases 606 
Zika Virus Infection 520 
Dengue Fever 206 
Guillain-Barre Syndrome 195 
Chikungunya Fever 155 
In the results, several diseases are associated with the Zika virus entity. Amongthem, Guillain-Barre Syndrome stands out because, unlike the others, it is not avector-borne disease. This makes its co-mention potentially unexpected andclinically significant, suggesting a possible complication rather than mere co-endemicity.
For this reason, it is helpful to get further details by exploring the textual contentthat mentions both Zika virus and Guillain–Barre syndrome. We can reuse thequery in listing 7.32 by replacing the first WHERE clause with n1.id= "C0318793"
AND n2.id = "C0018378", which are the UMLS ids of Zika virus and Guillain–Barre syndrome, respectively (we also removed from the results the “Co-occurringentity id” and the “Co-occurring entity name” fields because they are not useful in

this case). The cleaned results of this query, obtained by removing redundantresults, are shown in table 7.9.

"Zika and potential complications published on 12February 2016, six countries have reported an increase inthe incidence of cases of microcephaly (Brazil) andGuillain-Barre syndrome” 
sample_dataset-PublicUse/ECDCDocuments/zika virus/zika-virus-rapid-risk-assessment-11-april-2016.docx.pdf

The results state that Zika virus is one of the causes of Guillain–Barre syndrome.So, we expect ontologies such as SNOMED to include a fact such as Guillain-
Barre syndrome-[:CAUSATIVE_AGENT]->Zika virus. Let’s check by running thequery in listing 7.33 and replacing Zika virus disease (SNOMED ID 3928002)with Infectious neuronitis (the SNOMED term for Guillain–Barre syndrome;SNOMED ID 40956001) in the WHERE clause. The following listing shows a subsetof the results: multiple SNOMED ontology paths connect these entities, but mostof these paths do not represent meaningful connections between.
Listing 7.38 Paths connecting Zika virus and Infectious neuronitis
(Zika virus)<-[:CAUSATIVE_AGENT]-(Congenital Zika virus infection) 
-[:PATHOLOGICAL_PROCESS_(ATTRIBUTE)]->(Infectious process (qualifier valu
e)) 
<-[:PATHOLOGICAL_PROCESS_(ATTRIBUTE)]-(Reactivation of hepatitis B viral 
hepatitis (disorder)) 
-[:ASSOCIATED_MORPHOLOGY]->(Inflammation) 
<-[:ASSOCIATED_MORPHOLOGY]-(Infectious neuronitis) 
 
(Zika virus)<-[:CAUSATIVE_AGENT]-(Zika virus disease) 
-[:CAUSATIVE_AGENT]->(Togavirus) 
<-[:CAUSATIVE_AGENT]-(Mosquito-borne flavivirus encephalitis) 
-[:ASSOCIATED_MORPHOLOGY]->(Inflammation) 
<-[:ASSOCIATED_MORPHOLOGY]-(Infectious neuronitis)

In the first entry, Zika virus is connected to Infectious neuronitis because Zikavirus is the causative agent of Congenital Zika virus infection, which is aninfectious process. The issue is that the Infectious process (qualifier value) node isconnected to multiple contagious processes, such as Reactivation of hepatitis Bviral hepatitis (disorder). This disorder is associated with inflammation, which isalso a morphological manifestation of Infectious neuronitis. Similar reasoning canbe applied to the second entry in listing 7.38. These paths were retrieved becausethey include hub nodes, such as Infectious process (qualifier value) andInflammation, which are connected to a massive number of nodes related toinfectious processes.
One solution is to filter out paths that include these hub nodes. To do so, we canuse graph data science algorithms provided by the Neo4j Graph Data ScienceLibrary (GDS), which offers tools to compute the centrality of a node in the graph.To run this algorithm, the first step is to create a graph projection that includes therelevant set of nodes and relationships to perform our analysis. In this case, wewant to focus on the SNOMED ontology graph, and we can run the followingcode.
Listing 7.39 Creating a projection on the SNOMED ontology
CALL gds.graph.project( 
  'snomedGraph', 
  'SnomedEntity', 
  'SNOMED_RELATION' 
) 
YIELD 
  graphName AS graph, 
  relationshipProjection AS knowsProjection, 
  nodeCount AS nodes, 
  relationshipCount AS rels;
After generating the projection, we can run the degree algorithm in streamingmode to retrieve the most-connected nodes and use this result to filter out pathsthat are not relevant for our purpose.

Listing 7.40 Filtering out hub nodes
CALL gds.degree.stream('snomedGraph') 
YIELD nodeId, score 
WITH gds.util.asNode(nodeId).name AS name, score AS degree 
ORDER BY degree DESC 
LIMIT 350 
WITH collect(name) AS hub_nodes  #1 
 
MATCH (s1), (s2) 
WHERE s1.id = "3928002" AND s2.id = "40956001" 
WITH s1,  
     s2, 
     allShortestPaths((s1)-[:SNOMED_RELATION*1..8]-(s2)) AS paths, 
    hub_nodes  #2 
UNWIND paths AS path 
WITH relationships(path) AS path_edges, 
nodes(path) AS path_nodes, 
hub_nodes 
WITH  
[n IN path_nodes | n.name] AS node_names, 
[r IN path_edges | COALESCE(r.type, 'IS_A')] AS rel_types,  #3 
[n IN path_edges | startnode(n).name] AS rel_starts,  #4 
hub_nodes 
WHERE NOT any(x IN node_names WHERE x IN hub_nodes)  #5 
WITH [i IN range(0, size(node_names) - 1) | 
CASE 
WHEN i = size(node_names) - 1 
THEN '(' + node_names[i] + ')'  #6 
WHEN node_names[i] = rel_starts[i] 
THEN '(' + node_names[i] + ')' + '-[:' + rel_types[i] + ']->'  #7 
ELSE '(' + node_names[i] + ')' + '<-[:' + rel_types[i] + ']-'  #8 
END 
] AS string_paths 
RETURN DISTINCT apoc.text.join(string_paths, '') AS `Extracted paths`
#1 Collects the top 350 high-degree nodes (central hubs) #2 Finds all shortest paths (1–8 hops) between the two SNOMED concept nodes #3 Defaults the relationship type to “IS_A” if it's missing #4 Retrieves the name of the source node for each relationship to determine directionality in the finalstring #5 Excludes any path that passes through a hub node #6 Marks the end of the path #7 Renders a forward (outgoing) relationship between the current node and the next #8 Renders a backward (incoming) relationship from the next node to the current one 
This query combines the nodes’ degree computation with the detection of relevantpaths connecting two entities. Paths that include nodes with a higher degree are

excluded from the results. The next listing shows the results after this filteringprocess.

(Zika virus disease)-[:IS_A]->(Disease due to Flavivirus) 
<-[:IS_A]-(Acute hepatitis C) 
-[:IS_A]->(Acute inflammatory disorder) 
<-[:IS_A]-(Infectious neuronitis)

tive) 
-[:IS_A]->(Context-dependent finding (context-dependent category)) 
<-[:IS_A]-(History of Guillain Barre syndrome (situation)) 
-[:ASSOCIATED_FINDING]->(Infectious neuronitis) 
 
(Zika virus disease)-[:IS_A]->(Viral disease) 
<-[:IS_A]-(Common cold)-[:IS_A]->(Acute inflammatory disorder) 
<-[:IS_A]-(Infectious neuronitis) 
 
(Zika virus disease)-[:IS_A]->(Viral disease) 
<-[:IS_A]-(VHF – Viral haemorrhagic fever) 
-[:IS_A]->(Acute inflammatory disorder) 
<-[:IS_A]-(Infectious neuronitis) 
 
(Zika virus disease)<-[:ASSOCIATED_FINDING]-(Presumptive recent Zika posi
tive) 
-[:IS_A]->(Context-dependent finding (context-dependent category)) 
<-[:IS_A]-(History of Guillain Barre syndrome (situation)) 
-[:ASSOCIATED_FINDING]->(Infectious neuronitis) 
 
(Zika virus disease)-[:IS_A]->(Viral disease) 
<-[:TEMPORALLY_FOLLOWS]-(Transient paroxysmal cold hemoglobinuria) 
-[:PATHOLOGICAL_PROCESS_(ATTRIBUTE)]->(AI – autoimmune) 
<-[:PATHOLOGICAL_PROCESS_(ATTRIBUTE)]-(Infectious neuronitis) 
 
(Zika virus disease)-[:IS_A]->(Viral disease) 
<-[:DUE_TO]-(Erythema multiforme caused by virus (disorder)) 
-[:PATHOLOGICAL_PROCESS_(ATTRIBUTE)]->(AI – autoimmune) 
<-[:PATHOLOGICAL_PROCESS_(ATTRIBUTE)]-(Infectious neuronitis) 
 
(Zika virus disease)-[:IS_A]->(Viral disease) 
<-[:AFTER]-(Transient paroxysmal cold hemoglobinuria) 
-[:PATHOLOGICAL_PROCESS_(ATTRIBUTE)]->(AI – autoimmune) 
<-[:PATHOLOGICAL_PROCESS_(ATTRIBUTE)]-(Infectious neuronitis)

This time, we retrieved a result set of 9 entries, compared to the 11,185 pathsdetected with the base query. However, the results still include general entitiessuch as Viral disease, which connects Zika virus disease to random viral diseasesthat can be used to connect Zika virus disease to Infectious neuronitis. In otherwords, a direct connection between these entities is not encoded in the SNOMEDontology. This is a typical example in which the co-occurrence of entities definedin the KG can potentially be used to enrich a domain ontology in a virtuous circle.
This mechanism can be exponentially enhanced by extracting meaningfulrelationships from the text. In this approach, the starting point is represented by theextracted relationships, which are more specific than the co-occurrenceconnection; see figure 7.17.
Figure 7.17 Mental model describing the process of uncovering new knowledge. In this case, “Zikavirus” and “Guillain-Barre syndrome” appear multiple times in the same sentences, but the medicalontologies do not provide any relevant connections between these entities.

Summary
Named entity disambiguation (NED) lets us connect entities mentioned in thetext to a reference knowledge base.
Combining NED with KG technologies opens new opportunities to developadvanced services in critical domains.
Constructing a KG requires multiple steps, including defining the schema,ingesting documents, disambiguating entities from these documents,integrating domain ontologies, mapping extracted entities, and generating co-occurrence relationships between entities located in the same sentence.
Advanced analysis can be performed on the KG to support different use casesin the application domain: conceptual search, structured knowledge-basedsearch, KG-based interpretability and discovery, and uncovering newknowledge.

8 NED with open LLMs and
domain ontologies
This chapter covers
Understanding the limitations of traditional NED tools
Combining general-purpose LLMs and domain ontologies for NED
Performing multistep disambiguation with shortest-paths detection,
path-to-text translation, and textual paths summarization
Chapter 7 is focused on named entity disambiguation (NED), highlighting
the role of scispaCy, a specialized natural language processing (NLP) tool
built on the spaCy framework. This tool is designed to process documents
and publications by providing pretrained models in the biomedical domain.
8.1 Understanding limitations of traditional NED
systems
scispaCy incorporates vocabularies and ontologies, such as the Unified
Medical Language System (UMLS), that provide canonical entities useful
for disambiguating mentions in the text. However, this approach has some
limitations:
It is designed for a particular application domain: the biomedical field.
It presents challenges in expanding and updating the reference
knowledge base to incorporate new entities and terms.
It fails to fully use the extensive information available in the knowledge
base.
It doesn’t use the existing relationships and paths between entities for
the disambiguation task.

To understand the effect of this last point, let’s recap the example we
discussed at the beginning of chapter 7, which used this quote from the
European Centre for Disease Prevention and Control (ECDC):
In the week of 13 April, Belize reported for the first time mosquito-
borne Zika virus transmission. Update on the observed increase of

Microcephaly and other fetal malformations potentially associated with

But now let’s test the following slightly different example that doesn’t

Zika belongs to the Flaviviridae virus family, and it is spread by Aedes

like chikungunya fever often experience symptoms like viral myalgia,

infectious edema, and infective conjunctivitis. Severe outcomes of Zika
are due to its capacity to cross the placental barrier during pregnancy,
causing microcephaly and congenital malformations.
Compared to the previous example, there are no words supporting the

The model disambiguates “Zika” as the entity “C0276289 Zika Virus
Infection” in the first and the third sentences, but it doesn’t detect a target
entity for the mention in the second sentence.
This chapter addresses these limitations with a novel approach that uses
open large language models (LLMs) and domain ontologies. Unlike domain-
based tools such as scispaCy, this approach can be used in other application
domains in which we can use rich ontologies.
8.2 Ingesting the domain ontology
To drive the disambiguation process, we will use the SNOMED
(Systematized Nomenclature of Medicine) ontology introduced in chapter 7.
As a reminder, SNOMED is a multilingual clinical terminology repository
encompassing more than 450,000 concepts and a rich set of relationship
types. For our example scenario, we will again use these two files:

sct2_Description_Full-en_US1000124_20220901.txt (entity names and
aliases, and relationships between entities) and
sct2_Relationship_Full_US1000124 _20220901.txt (numerical codes
identifying entities and relationships).
NOTE  For examples from these files, see section 7.5.2.
Figure 8.1 illustrates the SNOMED hierarchical structure and the
propagation of information through the nodes. Listings 8.3–8.5 do the
following, respectively: create nodes and relationships in Neo4j from
sct2_Relationship_Full_US1000124_20220901.txt, extract names and
aliases from sct2_Description_Full-en_US1000124_20220901.txt, and
follow the hierarchical structure to propagate information from first-level
nodes to deeper nodes.
NOTE  For annotated versions of these listings and more details, see
section 7.6.4. The complete example code is available in the book’s
online repository.

Figure 8.1 A sample of SNOMED’s hierarchical structure. Nodes on deeper levels can be
categorized using information from first-level nodes, which are the ontology’s archetypal
entities.

Listing 8.3 Ingesting SNOMED: loading relationships
[...] 
class SnomedRelationshipsImporter(BaseImporter):  
  [...]   
  def set_constraints(self):  
    queries = [ 
        ( 
            "CREATE CONSTRAINT IF NOT EXISTS FOR (n:SnomedEntity) " 
            "REQUIRE n.id IS UNIQUE" 
        ), 
        ( 
            "CREATE INDEX snomedNodeName IF NOT EXISTS " 
            "FOR (n:SnomedEntity) ON (n.name)" 
        ), 
        ( 
            "CREATE INDEX snomedRelationId IF NOT EXISTS " 
            "FOR ()-[r:SNOMED_RELATION]-() ON (r.id)" 
        ), 
        ( 
            "CREATE INDEX snomedRelationType IF NOT EXISTS " 
            "FOR ()-[r:SNOMED_RELATION]-() ON (r.type)" 
        ), 
        ( 
            "CREATE INDEX snomedRelationUmls IF NOT EXISTS " 
            "FOR ()-[r:SNOMED_RELATION]-() ON (r.umls)" 
        ), 
    ] 
 
 
    for q in queries: 
      self.connection.query(q, db=self.db) 
 
  def import_snomed_rels(self):  
    query = """ 
       UNWIND $batch as item 
       MERGE (e1:SnomedEntity {id: item.sourceId}) 
       MERGE (e2:SnomedEntity {id: item.destinationId}) 
       MERGE (e1)-[:SNOMED_RELATION {id: item.typeId}]->(e2) 
       FOREACH(ignoreMe IN CASE WHEN item.typeId = '116680003'  
       ↪ THEN [true] ELSE [] END| 
         MERGE (e1)-[:SNOMED_IS_A]->(e2)  
       ) 
       """ 

 
size = self.get_csv_size(snomedRels_file)  
self.batch_store(snomed_rels_query, self.get_rows(snomedRels_file),
 size=size)

Listing 8.4 Ingesting SNOMED: loading names and aliases
[...] 
class SnomedNamesImporter(BaseImporter): 
  [...] 
 
  def import_snomed_names(self, snomedNames_file): 
        snomed_names_concepts_query = """ 
        UNWIND $batch as item 
        MATCH (e1:SnomedEntity) 
        -[r:SNOMED_RELATION {id: item.conceptId}]-> 
        (e2:SnomedEntity) 
        WHERE item.conceptId <> '116680003' AND r.id = item.conceptI
d  
        SET r.type = CASE  
                WHEN r.type IS NULL THEN item.termAsType 
                ELSE r.type END,  
            r.aliases = CASE  
                WHEN item.termAsType IN r.aliases THEN r.aliases 
                ELSE coalesce(r.aliases,[]) + item.termAsType END 
        """ 
 
        snomed_names_entities_query = """ 
        UNWIND $batch as item 
        MATCH (e:SnomedEntity {id: item.conceptId}) 
        SET e.name = CASE  
                WHEN e.name IS NULL THEN item.term 
                ELSE e.name END,  
            e.aliases = CASE  
                WHEN item.term in e.aliases THEN  e.aliases 
                ELSE coalesce(e.aliases, []) + item.term END  
        """ 
        size = self.get_csv_size(snomedNames_file) 
        self.batch_store( 
          snomed_names_concepts_query, 
          self.get_rows(snomedNames_file), 
         size=size) 
        self.batch_store( 
          snomed_names_entities_query, 
          self.get_rows(snomedNames_file), 
          size=size) 
[...]

Listing 8.5 Ingesting SNOMED: labeling propagation from first-level nodes
[...] 
class SnomedLabelPropagator():     
[...]   
 
  def get_rows(self): 
    propagation_query = """ 
      MATCH p=(n:SnomedEntity)<-[:SNOMED_IS_A]-(m:SnomedEntity)  
      WHERE n.id= "138875005" // Root node 
      WITH distinct m as first_node 
 
      CALL apoc.path.expandConfig(first_node, { // #A 
              relationshipFilter: '<SNOMED_IS_A', 
                minLevel: 1, 
                maxLevel: -1, 
                uniqueness: 'RELATIONSHIP_GLOBAL' 
            }) yield path 
 
     UNWIND nodes(path) as other_level // #B 
     WITH first_node, collect(DISTINCT other_level) as uniques 
             UNWIND uniques as unique_other_level 
             WITH first_node,unique_other_level 
             WHERE not first_node.name in coalesce(unique_other_leve
l.type,[]) 
 
             RETURN unique_other_level.id as id, first_node.name as 
label - C 
            """ 
 
   with self._driver.session(database=self._database) as session: 
     result = session.run(query=propagation_query) 
     for record in iter(result): 
        yield dict(record) 
[...]
The SNOMED_IS_A relationship has been used to propagate the semantic types
through the tree structure by using the hierarchical connections between
entities.
8.3 Setting up the model with Ollama and Llama
3.1 8B

In previous chapters, we explored how to use OpenAI APIs to perform NLP
tasks. Now, we extend that knowledge by deploying a NED system locally
using Ollama and Llama 3.1 8B (released by Meta).
Ollama is an open source tool that lets users run LLMs directly on their local
machines. By running models locally, we gain full control over our data
while reducing latency and dependency on external providers. Llama 3.1 8B
is an open source LLM with 8 billion parameters. It supports a context
length of up to 128,000 tokens and is optimized for multilingual information
processing. It is also designed for efficient deployment on consumer-grade
hardware.
To deploy the Llama 3.1 8B model on your local machine, you will first
need to download and install Ollama. The tool is compatible with macOS,
Linux, and Windows, and the installation files are available at
https://ollama.com/. Ollama offers both command-line and graphical user
interface (GUI) options; we used the following command-line instructions to
download and deploy Llama 3.1 8B for our NED system.
Listing 8.6 Ollama commands to download and install Llama 3.1 8B
ollama serve 
ollama pull llama3.1:latest
Ollama offers built-in compatibility with the OpenAI Chat Completions API,
so we can interact directly with our locally deployed model using Python
code like that in previous chapters. This simplifies the process of integrating
the model into our NED system. The next listing shows the Python class
needed to interact with our model.

Listing 8.7 Running our Llama 3.1 8B model in Python
from openai import OpenAI 
 
class LLM_Model(): 
    def __init__(self, url='http://localhost:11434/v1', key="defaul
t"): 
        self.client = OpenAI( 
          base_url= url,  #1 
          api_key = key, #2 
        ) 
 
    def generate(self, messages): 
        response = self.client.chat.completions.create( 
            model="llama3.1:latest",  #3 
            messages=messages, 
            temperature=0, 
            max_tokens=4000, 
            top_p=1, 
            frequency_penalty=0, 
            presence_penalty=0, 
        ) 
        # It assumes as response the ChatGPT API format 
        return response.choices[0].message.content
#1 Default URL through which the model is served 
#2 “api_key” is required for the OpenAI Chat Completions API but is not used for open models.
#3 Specifies llama3.1:latest, downloaded by Ollama 
NOTE  We obtained our results for the example, generated using the
prompts in the following sections, in October 2024 using the latest
version of the Llama 3.1 model.
Using a general-purpose model like Llama 3.1 for NED will demonstrate the
potential of LLMs to perform well in niche areas when combined with
domain-specific ontologies. In the next section, we break down this process
and show how the system can interpret and disambiguate entities in complex
biomedical texts, facilitating information extraction and analysis.
8.4 End-to-end NED process

Figure 8.2 shows the mental model describing our example’s NED process
from the input document to the disambiguated mentions. The process begins
with an input document containing unstructured text, which is analyzed by
an LLM-based named entity recognition (NER) component. Here, the LLM
identifies and labels relevant biomedical entities in the input text using the
knowledge embedded in the domain ontology. For instance, a term like
“Zika” can be recognized as a Disease concept according to SNOMED. This
step transforms raw text into structured data, which will be processed in
subsequent stages.

Figure 8.2 Workflow for a NED system designed to use LLMs and domain-specific ontologies,
such as SNOMED, for biomedical text processing. Each stage of this workflow involves
interactions to accurately disambiguate entities in the input text.
Next, the system moves to the NED candidate selection (CS) stage. A full-
text search mechanism generates a list of possible matches for each
identified entity mention. For instance, the term “Zika” may correspond to
several entities in SNOMED, such as Zika Virus, Zika Virus Infection, and
Congenital Zika Virus Infection. This step sets up a pool of potential
disambiguation targets; the system will evaluate them in the following phase
to find the most accurate match.

In the final stage, NED candidate disambiguation (CD), the LLM refines its
selection to determine the most precise entity match for each mention. A
multistep approach identifies the shortest path between candidates in the
ontology structure; it then translates and summarizes relevant path details to
support disambiguation with contextual knowledge and ensure that each
entity mentioned in the input document is mapped accurately to its
corresponding disambiguated entity in the ontology.
This LLM-driven approach integrates domain-specific ontologies at each
step of the disambiguation process. By incorporating the hierarchical and
relational structures of the ontology, the model can make more informed
decisions about entity classification and disambiguation, especially in
complex cases where terms may have multiple meanings or associations.
8.4.1 Named entity recognition
The goal of NER is to identify and classify named entities mentioned in
unstructured text into predefined categories, such as diseases, organisms, and
procedures. As discussed in previous chapters, one practical approach is to
use prompt engineering, where the types of entities we are interested in are
explicitly defined in the prompt. Often, a data scientist or data engineer
works with a domain expert to identify and define these entities.
In our scenario, we incorporate SNOMED’s structured medical knowledge
to enable the LLM to perform more precise and contextually aware entity
recognition in biomedical texts. Figure 8.3 illustrates the input and output of
the NER.
NER requires us to retrieve all the predefined categories from the ontology.
The following query retrieves the categories from SNOMED.
Listing 8.8 Retrieving predefined categories from SNOMED
MATCH (n:SnomedEntity) 
UNWIND n.type as named_entity 
WITH DISTINCT named_entity, count(named_entity) as num_of_entities 
ORDER BY num_of_entities DESC 
RETURN collect(named_entity) as named_entities

We can use the results from this query in our prompt for the NER task.
Listing 8.9 is a simplified version of the prompt messages we defined for
this purpose; the full prompt is in code repository.
Figure 8.3 The first stage of NED is NER. In our scenario, named entities are derived directly
from the ontology. In SNOMED, categories are defined by the ontology’s first-level nodes, whose
information is propagated to all the other nodes.

Listing 8.9 Simplified prompt for NER
system = """You are an assistant capable of extracting named entitie
s in the 
↪ medical domain.  
Your task is to extract ALL single mentions of named entities from t
he text.  
You must only use one of the pre-defined entities from the following 
list: 
{named_entities}.  
No other entity categories are allowed.  
For each sentence, extract the named entities and present the output 
in  
valid JSON format""".format(named_entities=named_entities)) 
 
input = """Risk factors for rhinocerebral mucormycosis include poorl
y 
controlled diabetes mellitus and severe immunosuppression.""" 
 
assistant = [ 
  { 
    "sentence": """Risk factors for rhinocerebral mucormycosis inclu
de 
 poorly controlled diabetes mellitus and severe immunosuppressio
n.""", 
    "entities": [ 
      { 
        "id": 0, 
        "mention": "Risk factors", 
        "label": "Events" 
      }, 
      { 
        "id": 1, 
        "mention": "rhinocerebral mucormycosis", 
        "label": "Disease" 
      }, 
      { 
        "id": 2, 
        "mention": "poorly controlled diabetes mellitus", 
        "label": "Disease" 
      }, 
      { 
        "id": 3, 
        "mention": "severe immunosuppression", 

        "label": "Qualifier value" 
      } 
    ] 
  } 
]
This prompt is structured as follows:
System instruction—The system message says to extract occurrences of
named entities that belong to categories in the medical domain from the
SNOMED ontology, avoiding irrelevant or out-of-scope categories.
Input text—In this example, the input text discusses risk factors for a
medical condition (rhinocerebral mucormycosis), listing conditions
such as diabetes mellitus and immunosuppression that are medical
terms which need to be recognized.
Assistant output—The system responds with structured JSON output
that contains the following fields:
sentence—The system processes text sentence by sentence to ensure
that it analyzes each unit of meaning individually.
entities—The output includes an array of identified entities. Each
entry contains an ID to uniquely identify the entity in the sentence, a
mention of the named entity found in the text (e.g., “rhinocerebral
mucormycosis”), and a label that classifies the entity according to a
SNOMED category, such as Disease.
Here’s an example of input text passed to the LLM instructed with the NER
prompt.

he 
placental barrier during pregnancy, causing microcephaly 
and congenital malformations""".

From this result, we can identify and classify three distinct entities:
“Zika”—Identified as an Organism, with its position in the sentence
spanning from character 19 to 22.
“Microcephaly”—Labeled a Clinical finding (finding), indicating that it
is a medical condition. This mention appears from character 105 to 116.
“Congenital malformations”—Also labeled a Clinical finding (finding).
It is located between characters 122 and 145 in the sentence.

LLMs have trouble accurately detecting the starting and ending characters of
mentions in a sentence. For this reason, we generated the start and end
fields in post-processing with the following Python function.
Listing 8.12 Python function to compute starting and ending characters of a mention
def find_all_mention_indices(self, string, substring): 
  indices = [] 
  start_index = 0 
 
  while True: 
    start_index = string.find(substring, start_index) 
 
    if start_index == -1: 
      break  # No more occurrences found 
 
    end_index = start_index + len(substring) - 1 
    indices.append((start_index, end_index)) 
 
    # Move start_index forward to search for the next occurrence 
    start_index += len(substring) 
 
  return indices
This function identifies the position of the mention, which is information
recognized by traditional NER systems.
8.4.2 Candidate selection
The second phase of the NED process is CS, which identifies relevant
entities or concepts that could match the intended meaning of each identified
named entity. Figure 8.4 illustrates the input and output of this phase,
highlighting how candidate entities are selected.

Figure 8.4 The second stage of NED is candidate selection. For each entity mention detected in
the previous step, this stage retrieves potential candidates that may refer to it.
As shown in the following listing, the input for CS consists of the mentions
annotated in the input text by the NER process, along with the domain
ontology. The output is a list of one or more candidate entities associated
with each mention.
We do not use the LLM in this step for two reasons. First, we want to
retrieve candidates directly from the domain ontology rather than rely on
knowledge embedded in the LLM. Second, the size of the ontology prevents
us from loading it in its entirety in a prompt. So, to perform CS efficiently,
we use Neo4j’s full-text search capabilities, which can identify strings in the
ontology that closely match each mention.

Listing 8.13 Python class for CS
class CandidateSelection: 
[...] 
  def full_text_query(self): 
    query = """ 
            CALL db.index.fulltext.queryNodes("names", $fulltextQuer
y, 
            ↪ {limit: $limit}) 
            YIELD node 
            WHERE node:SnomedEntity AND ANY(x IN node.type  
            ↪ WHERE x IN $labels) 
            RETURN distinct node.name AS candidate_name, node.id  
            ↪ AS candidate_id 
            """ 
 
    return query 
 
  def generate_full_text_query(self, input): 
    full_text_query = "" 
    words = [el for el in input.split() if el] 
 
    if len(words) > 1: 
      for word in words[:-1]: 
        full_text_query += f" {word}~0.80 AND " 
        full_text_query += f" {words[-1]}~0.80" 
    else: 
      full_text_query = words[0] + "~0.80" 
 
    return full_text_query.strip() [...]
We specify the $labels parameter to reduce the query’s search space. These
labels are collected from the output of the NER phase, forcing the system to
identify only a subset of entities that are relevant to the type of entities
mentioned.
NOTE  Although the full-text search mechanism offers a viable
solution, it can be enhanced by incorporating a vector-based search to
retrieve additional candidates that may not be identified through text
matching.

The JSON result of the query when we pass “Zika” as an input term is
shown next.
